blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396027621-872667077.png
blocks.alt: Splitting a monolith with one shared database into microservices where each service owns its own database

blocks.content: The story starts the moment you decided to split your monolith. You had one database. Transactions were easy BEGIN, do everything, COMMIT. Atomicity was free. Consistency was guaranteed by the database engine.
Then you split into microservices. Order Service has its own database. Payment Service has its own database. Inventory Service has its own database. Notification Service has its own database.
Now a customer places an order. You need to:
["Create the order record","Charge the payment","Reserve the inventory","Send a confirmation email"]
items: Create the order record
Charge the payment
Reserve the inventory
Send a confirmation email

blocks.content: All four must succeed together. If payment fails, the order shouldn't exist. If inventory is out of stock, the payment shouldn't be charged. In a monolith, one transaction handles this. In microservices, there is no such thing as a transaction that spans four separate databases. You could use Two-Phase Commit. But 2PC requires a distributed coordinator, holds locks across all four services simultaneously, blocks on coordinator failure, and performs terribly under load. Most microservices teams consider it impractical.
The Saga pattern is the alternative the industry actually uses.
1. What is a Saga?

A Saga is a sequence of local transactions one per service where each transaction publishes an event or sends a message that triggers the next step. If any step fails, the saga executes compensating transactions to undo the work already done by previous steps.

No global locks. No distributed coordinator holding everything open. Each service commits independently to its own database. The atomicity is eventual the system will eventually reach a consistent state, either fully committed or fully rolled back.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785305476037-879452605.png
blocks.alt: A saga as a sequence of local transactions per service, with compensating transactions run in reverse on failure

blocks.content: The compensating transactions are the price you pay. For every forward step, you must write a corresponding undo step. Charging a payment is compensated by issuing a refund.

Creating an order is compensated by cancelling it. Reserving inventory is compensated by releasing it. These compensations must themselves be reliable which means they're not simple rollbacks, they're real business operations that go through their own retry logic.
2. Two implementations Of Saga Pattern

There are two completely different ways to coordinate a saga. They have opposite trade-offs and different failure characteristics. Choosing between them is one of the most important design decisions when implementing sagas.
1. Choreography: services react to events

In choreography, there is no central coordinator. Each service listens for events and reacts by doing its work and publishing the next event. Services don't know about each other they only know about events.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785305477704-524731293.png
blocks.alt: Choreography: each service publishes and listens to events on a shared event bus with no central coordinator

blocks.content: The flow starts when the Order Service creates an order and publishes an OrderCreated event. The Payment Service listens to this event, processes the payment, and publishes a PaymentCharged event. Next, the Inventory Servicereceives this event and checks whether the required stock is available.

At this point, the flow can go in two directions. If stock is available, the Inventory Service publishes a StockReserved event, which is consumed by the Notification Service to send a confirmation notification. This represents the successful completion of the saga.
If stock is not available, the Inventory Service publishes a StockReservationFailed event.

This triggers the Refund Payment process, which refunds the customer's payment and publishes a PaymentRefunded event. After receiving this event, the Order Service cancels the order, thereby undoing the previously completed operations.

Each service is completely autonomous. Payment Service doesn't know Inventory Service exists. It just knows: "when I successfully charge a payment, publish a PaymentCharged event." What happens next is someone else's problem.
Choreography is good when:

["You have a small number of steps (2–4 services)","Services are genuinely independent teams who don't want to coordinate","You want maximum decoupling","The saga flows in one direction without complex branching"]
items: You have a small number of steps (2–4 services)
Services are genuinely independent teams who don't want to coordinate
You want maximum decoupling
The saga flows in one direction without complex branching

blocks.content: Choreography gets painful when:

["You need to understand the full saga flow, it's spread across 6 services with no single view","You need to debug a stuck saga which service dropped the event?","You add a new service and need to find all the events it needs to react to","The flow has conditional branches (\"if premium user, skip payment and charge monthly\")"]
items: You need to understand the full saga flow, it's spread across 6 services with no single view
You need to debug a stuck saga which service dropped the event?
You add a new service and need to find all the events it needs to react to
The flow has conditional branches ("if premium user, skip payment and charge monthly")

blocks.content: The core problem with choreography at scale: nobody owns the saga. To understand what's happening to order #12345, you need to query logs across four different services and stitch them together by trace ID. This is fine at small scale. It becomes genuinely painful at large scale.
2. Orchestration: one coordinator drives everything

In orchestration, a dedicated Saga Orchestrator service controls the entire workflow. It knows every step, calls each service directly, waits for the response, and decides what to do next. Services don't know about each other they just receive commands and report results to the orchestrator.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785305479372-41532925.png
blocks.alt: Orchestration: a Saga Orchestrator calls each service directly and waits for its response before deciding the next step

blocks.content: Important Terms in the Diagram
Before understanding the flow, let's understand what each component does.

1. The Saga Orchestrator is the brain of the entire process. It controls the workflow, decides which service should be called next, tracks the progress of the transaction, and handles failures. Instead of services communicating with each other directly, every service communicates through the orchestrator.

2. The Saga State Database stores the current state of the saga. For example, it keeps track of whether the order was created, payment was completed, inventory was reserved, or the transaction failed. If the orchestrator crashes, it can read the saved state and continue from where it stopped instead of starting again.
3. The Order Service is responsible for creating the order in the system. Once the order is successfully created, it returns a success response to the orchestrator.
4. The Payment Service handles payment processing. It charges the customer and confirms whether the payment was successful or failed.
5. The Inventory Service manages product stock. Its job is to reserve the required items so that they cannot be purchased by someone else.
6. Notification Service: The Notification Service sends emails, SMS messages, or push notifications to inform the customer about the order status.

7. Persist Saga State: This means storing the latest saga progress in the Saga State Database. After every successful step, the orchestrator updates the state so recovery is possible if something goes wrong.
8. A Compensation is an undo operation. If a later step fails, previously completed steps must be reversed to maintain consistency.
Examples:
["Payment completed → Compensation = Refund Payment","Order created → Compensation = Cancel Order"]
items: Payment completed → Compensation = Refund Payment
Order created → Compensation = Cancel Order

blocks.content: 9. Saga Completed: This state means all services executed successfully and the business transaction finished without any errors.
Working
Suppose a customer places an order on an e-commerce website.

The request first reaches the Saga Orchestrator. The orchestrator creates a new saga instance and immediately saves the initial state in the Saga State DB. This allows the system to recover if a crash occurs later.

The orchestrator then calls the Order Service. The Order Service creates a new order and returns a success response. The orchestrator receives the response and updates the Saga State DB to indicate that the order has been created successfully.

Next, the orchestrator calls the Payment Service. The Payment Service charges the customer and returns either success or failure. If payment succeeds, the orchestrator stores the updated state and moves to the next step.
If payment fails, the orchestrator triggers the compensation action Cancel Order because an order should not exist without a successful payment. The saga is then marked as failed.

If payment succeeds, the orchestrator calls the Inventory Service. The Inventory Service reserves the required stock. If inventory reservation succeeds, the orchestrator updates the state and proceeds further. However, if inventory reservation fails because the item is out of stock, the orchestrator starts compensation.

Since payment was already completed, it first performs Refund Payment. After refunding the payment, it performs Cancel Order. Once all completed actions have been reversed, the saga is marked as failed.

If inventory reservation succeeds, the orchestrator calls the Notification Service. This service sends an email or SMS confirmation to the customer. When the notification is sent successfully, the orchestrator marks the saga as Completed and stores the final state in the Saga State Database.
The key idea is that the Saga Orchestrator always knows the current state of the transaction and controls every step. Whenever a service succeeds, it moves forward.

The orchestrator is a state machine. At any point it knows: which step is currently executing, what the result of each completed step was, and what to do next. This state is persisted to a database after every transition if the orchestrator crashes and restarts, it reads its last known state and continues.
Orchestration is good when:

["You have complex flows with branching logic (if premium user do X, else do Y)","You need a single place to see the state of any saga","You need to debug failures easily (one service, one log, one state record)","You have many steps (5+ services)","You need human approval steps in the middle of the flow"]
items: You have complex flows with branching logic (if premium user do X, else do Y)
You need a single place to see the state of any saga
You need to debug failures easily (one service, one log, one state record)
You have many steps (5+ services)
You need human approval steps in the middle of the flow

blocks.content: Orchestration gets painful when:

["The orchestrator becomes a god object that knows too much about every service","The orchestrator is a single point of failure (mitigated by HA deployment)","Services become coupled to the orchestrator's command format"]
items: The orchestrator becomes a god object that knows too much about every service
The orchestrator is a single point of failure (mitigated by HA deployment)
Services become coupled to the orchestrator's command format

blocks.content: 3. Choreography vs Orchestration
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785305480963-142829735.png
blocks.alt: Choreography (event-driven, decentralized) compared side by side with Orchestration (central coordinator driving every service)

blocks.content: 4. Compensating transactions ( The hard part )
Compensation means undoing previously completed steps when a later step fails. However, not every step in a Saga is treated the same way.
A Compensatable Transaction is a step that can be undone. In the diagram, Create Order can be undone using Cancel Order, and Charge Payment can be undone using Refund Payment.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396027625-726578380.png
blocks.alt: Create Order and Charge Payment are compensatable steps that can be undone, Reserve Stock is the pivot point of no return, Send Email and Log are retriable

blocks.content: A Pivot Transaction is the point of no return. In the diagram, Reserve Stock is the pivot. Once stock is successfully reserved, the saga is committed and rolling back no longer makes sense.
A Retriable Transaction is any step after the pivot. In the diagram, Send Email and Log are retriable transactions. If they fail, we don't roll back; we simply keep retrying until they succeed.
The flow is: Create Order → Charge Payment → Reserve Stock (Pivot) → Send Email → Log.
If a failure happens before the pivot succeeds, the saga moves backward using compensations. For example, it will Refund Payment and then Cancel Order.
If the pivot succeeds, the saga moves forward. Even if Send Email or Log fails, the system keeps retrying those steps instead of undoing everything.
One important rule is that compensations must be idempotent, meaning they should be safe to run multiple times.
For example, if a refund is already completed, running the refund again should not charge or refund the customer twice.
Also, compensations can fail. If a refund fails because the payment gateway is down, the saga keeps retrying the refund until it succeeds.
5. Transactional Outbox Pattern
The diagram shows how a service can reliably publish events without losing them if a crash happens.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396027623-28910618.png
blocks.alt: Transactional Outbox Pattern: the order and outbox rows are written in one DB transaction, then a message relay polls the outbox and publishes to Kafka

blocks.content: Suppose the Order Service receives a request to create an order. A common mistake is to first save the order in the database and then publish an OrderCreated event to Kafka. If the service crashes after saving the order but before publishing the event, the order exists in the database but no event is sent. The saga gets stuck because other services never know the order was created.
The Transactional Outbox Pattern solves this problem.
When the Order Service processes the request, it performs one database transaction. Inside this transaction, it writes two records to the same database:
["The order data in the Orders Table","The event information in the Outbox Table"]
items: The order data in the Orders Table
The event information in the Outbox Table

blocks.content: Both records are saved together atomically. This means either both are committed successfully or both are rolled back if a failure occurs. There is never a situation where the order is saved but the event is missing.
After that, an Outbox Reader continuously checks the Outbox Table for new events. This reader can use CDC (Debezium) or simple database polling.
When it finds a new event, it publishes the event to Kafka or RabbitMQ.

Why is this useful?: If the service crashes after saving the order, the event is still safely stored in the Outbox Table. When the service comes back, the Outbox Reader will eventually read the event and publish it. This guarantees that the event is not lost.
6. The saga state machine
The diagram shows how the Saga Orchestrator tracks the progress of a transaction by saving its current state after every successful step.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396027624-289703910.png
blocks.alt: The saga state machine moving from STARTED through ORDER_CREATED, PAYMENT_CHARGED, STOCK_RESERVED to COMPLETED, or into COMPENSATING and ORDER_CANCELLED on failure

blocks.content: The saga starts with STARTED. After the order is created, the state becomes ORDER_CREATED.
When payment is successfully charged, the state changes to PAYMENT_CHARGED. After inventory is reserved, it moves to STOCK_RESERVED. If all steps succeed, the final state becomes COMPLETED.

If any step fails, the saga enters the COMPENSATING state. During this phase, compensation actions are executed to undo previously completed work. For example, the order may be cancelled, moving the state to ORDER_CANCELLED, and once all rollback actions finish, the saga reaches the COMPENSATED state.

The important point is that every state transition is saved in the database before moving to the next step. This means if the orchestrator crashes after payment is completed, it can restart, read the last saved state (PAYMENT_CHARGED), and continue from there instead of starting the entire process again.
7. What Sagas Do NOT Give You
blocks.text: 7. What Sagas Do NOT Give You

blocks.content: Sagas do not provide isolation like traditional ACID transactions. While a saga is running, other services can see partially completed data.
A dirty read can occur when some steps are completed and others are still pending. For example, an order may be created and payment charged, but inventory is not yet reserved.
A lost update can occur when multiple sagas update the same data simultaneously. For example, two customers may try to buy the last item in stock at the same time.

To handle these problems, systems use techniques such as semantic locks, which mark records as being processed, optimistic locking, which uses version numbers to detect conflicts, and commutative updates, where values are updated incrementally instead of being overwritten.
Key Point: Sagas provide consistency across services, but they do not provide transaction isolation. Additional mechanisms are needed to handle concurrent updates safely.

blocks.content: 9. Saga Implementation Tools

["Apache Kafka: the dominant event bus for choreography-based sagas. Topics per event type, consumer groups per service, at-least-once delivery, compacted topics for saga state.
","Temporal: purpose-built workflow engine for orchestration-based sagas. Handles all the durability, retry, and state persistence concerns automatically. You write saga logic as plain code; Temporal makes it durable. Used by Stripe, Netflix, Uber, Coinbase.
","AWS Step Functions: managed orchestration as a service. Define saga steps as a state machine in JSON. AWS handles execution, retry, error handling. Well-integrated with other AWS services.
","Eventuate Tram / Sagas: open source framework specifically for the saga pattern. Provides transactional outbox, saga orchestrator, and choreography support.
","Axon Framework: Java-based CQRS + event sourcing + saga framework. Popular in enterprise Java shops.
"]
items: Apache Kafka: the dominant event bus for choreography-based sagas. Topics per event type, consumer groups per service, at-least-once delivery, compacted topics for saga state.

Temporal: purpose-built workflow engine for orchestration-based sagas. Handles all the durability, retry, and state persistence concerns automatically. You write saga logic as plain code; Temporal makes it durable. Used by Stripe, Netflix, Uber, Coinbase.
AWS Step Functions: managed orchestration as a service. Define saga steps as a state machine in JSON. AWS handles execution, retry, error handling. Well-integrated with other AWS services.
Eventuate Tram / Sagas: open source framework specifically for the saga pattern. Provides transactional outbox, saga orchestrator, and choreography support.
Axon Framework: Java-based CQRS + event sourcing + saga framework. Popular in enterprise Java shops.

blocks.content: 10. Saga vs 2PC: when to use which
blocks.text: 10. Saga vs 2PC: when to use which

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785305488885-756686651.png
blocks.alt: Saga (local transactions, eventual consistency, no cross-service locks) compared with Two-Phase Commit (prepare and commit phases with locks held until commit)

blocks.content: The rule of thumb: if your services have separate databases and you're building microservices, use sagas. If you're doing cross-shard transactions within a single database system that supports it (CockroachDB, Spanner), use 2PC it's built in and the blocking window is milliseconds thanks to Raft-backed coordinators.
11. HLD Interview: Transaction Across Multiple Services
blocks.text: 11. HLD Interview: Transaction Across Multiple Services

blocks.content: We cannot use a traditional ACID transaction because each microservice has its own database. Two-Phase Commit is complex, slow, and does not scale well.
To solve this, I would use the Saga Pattern. Each service performs its own local transaction, and if a later step fails, compensation actions are used to undo previous work.
I would prefer Orchestration Saga because a central orchestrator manages the entire workflow, tracks progress, handles failures, and can resume from the last state after a crash.

For reliable event publishing, I would use the Transactional Outbox Pattern. Business data and events are saved in the same database transaction, and an Outbox Reader (Debezium CDC) publishes events to Kafka.
The trade-off is that we lose ACID isolation, so other services may see intermediate states. This is handled using semantic locks, optimistic locking, and idempotent compensations.
In production, tools like Temporal can be used to manage saga execution, retries, and recovery automatically.
In short: Saga + Orchestrator + Transactional Outbox + Kafka + Temporal is a common solution for handling distributed transactions in microservices.
